t: In an elective monarchy the crown passes by election rather than inheritance; the electors were usually few and powerful, and candidates often came from a single royal house.
The prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire, whose rights the Golden Bull of 1356 fixed in law, and the free elections of Poland–Lithuania are its best-known European forms.
Elections let electors bind each new ruler with conditions, but invited bribery, foreign meddling and disputed choices, and most elective crowns became hereditary or disappeared.
dyk: The word conclave, from the Latin for “with a key”, recalls how cardinals were locked in until they chose a pope, a rule imposed in 1274 after an election at Viterbo had dragged on for almost three years.
ev: The Fourth Council of Toledo rules that Visigothic kings be chosen by the nobles and the bishops
East Frankish magnates elect Conrad of Franconia king after the last Carolingian ruler, Louis the Child, dies
Emperor Charles IV’s Golden Bull fixes the seven prince-electors and election by majority
Albert II’s election begins three centuries in which the electors choose only Habsburgs, until 1740
The first free election of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth makes Henry of Valois king
The Bohemian estates depose the Habsburg Ferdinand and elect Frederick V of the Palatinate
The Holy Roman Empire is dissolved, and its college of electors ends with it
Malaya’s Conference of Rulers elects the first Yang di-Pertuan Agong for a five-year term

f.power: The elected monarch, usually for life, often bound by conditions the electors imposed as the price of the crown, such as electoral capitulations or the Polish pacta conventa
f.legitimacy: Choice by a recognised body of electors, usually from a royal house or a qualified class, sealed by oath, coronation or religious consecration
f.chosen: Elected on the ruler’s death or abdication, sometimes in his lifetime, by prince-electors, the assembled nobility, a council of rulers or cardinals; in Malaysia for a five-year term
f.examples: Holy Roman Empire (prince-electors until 1806), Kingdom of Bohemia (until 1627), Kingdom of Hungary (until 1687), Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (free elections 1573–1764), Mongol Empire (the kurultai), Malaysia (since 1957)
